abstract: Power and Progress argues that technology does not automatically benefit workers; historical patterns show that shared prosperity requires deliberate policy choices. The authors contend that AI could follow historical trajectories of concentrating economic gains among capital owners rather than distributing benefits broadly across society, making intentional policy decisions critical to determining technology's distributional outcomes.
keyFindings: Technology does not automatically benefit workers; outcomes depend on policy choices rather than technological inevitability.
Historical patterns demonstrate that technological gains have often concentrated among capital owners rather than being shared broadly.
AI could follow historical patterns of widening inequality if deliberate policy interventions are not implemented.
Shared prosperity from technological advancement requires intentional institutional and policy design.
